ground_truth_witness: p = 7 (so y = 2p = 14, f = (p-1)/2 = 3). This satisfies every hypothesis the proof's own sentence imposes: 7 is prime, 7 > 3, and f = 3 <= 4, i.e. the Bugeaud-Gyory conclusion "f <= 4" does not exclude it. Yet p = 7 is not p = 5. Exhaustive computation of the set S = { p prime : p > 3, (p-1)/2 <= 4 } gives S = {5, 7} (p = 5 with f = 2, p = 7 with f = 3), not the singleton {5} the proof asserts. Script output: "COUNTEREXAMPLE(S) FOUND: [7] ... Claim says: the surviving case set is {5}; here p = 7 != 5 is in the surviving set, so the set is {5, 7} (size 2 > 1). Corresponding omitted case: y = 2p = 14." As non-load-bearing context the script also confirms that the exponent-3 shape is not vacuously impossible over the rational integers (e.g. 1^3 - (-1)^3 = 2 = 2^1, 2^3 - (-2)^3 = 16 = 2^4), so f = 3 is not silently ruled out by the shape of the equation itself; the refutation, however, rests only on the enumeration.
ground_truth_flaw: In the final case y = 2p (p > 3 prime, f = (p-1)/2), the proof asserts that the Bugeaud–Győry bound applied to the equation ξ^f − ζ^f = 2^σ forces f ≤ 4 and that this "leaves only the case p = 5". The enumeration is incomplete: f ≤ 4 also admits f = 3, i.e. p = 7 (y = 14), so the reduction to a single remaining case p = 5 is false.
